title: Gender bias across LLMs is common and highly heterogeneous
abstract: Understanding gender biases in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important as these systems become embedded in decision-support tools with real consequences. Prior research has focused only on a small set of models, leaving open the extent to which gender biases are common and heterogeneous across LLMs. We address this gap across ten models released between April 2025 and June 2026, spanning nine vendors, using two paradigms: gender attribution to stereotyped phrases (Study 1) and moral judgment of abuse or torture against a woman or a man to prevent a catastrophic outcome (Study 2). In Study 1, two of ten models attributed masculine-stereotyped phrases to female writers more often than the reverse, while three models showed the opposite pattern. In Study 2, several models converged on a male-disadvantaging asymmetry that was directionally consistent with a documented human tendency to protect female targets from harm, though the specific conditions under which this asymmetry emerged varied by model; three other models, by contrast, showed no variation across conditions. These results indicate that gender-related biases are common in LLMs. Their direction and magnitude, however, are highly heterogeneous, to the point that some models behave in diametrically opposite ways to others. Bias auditing should therefore be treated as an ongoing, multi-vendor process, rather than a one-time assessment.

title: AI Representations of Mental Health Stigma: Quantifying the Gap Between AI Estimations and Human Perceptions Across Gender Groups Using GPT-Based LLMs
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mental health applications raises concerns about its potential to internalize and perpetuate societal biases. This research evaluates both disparities and misalignment in how large language models (LLMs), GPT-4 and GPT-5, represent perceptions of mental health across gender groups. The research comprises two studies. Study 1 applied widely adopted measures of Social Distance, Stereotypes, and Attitudes Toward Seeking Help to assess whether the AI models depict systematic gender differences. Study 2 compared AI estimations of Personal, Self, and Perceived Stigma with large-scale real-world human data from the Healthy Minds Study (N = 76,406) to evaluate alignment between AI estimations and human perceptions. Results from Study 1 showed the AI models consistently portrayed men as having the greatest desire for social distance from someone with mental health problems, relatively higher Stereotypes scores, and the least favorable attitudes toward help-seeking, compared with women and nonbinary individuals. Study 2 confirmed that this ordinal pattern partially aligned with human-reported data for Personal and Self Stigma. However, the AI models systematically underestimated Personal Stigma and Perceived Stigma while substantially overestimating Self Stigma for all gender groups. These findings reveal that, although the AI models have learned relative gender-based patterns reflecting human experiences to a certain extent, they function as distorted portrayals, highlighting the need for rigorous, context-specific validation against real-world data to ensure AI's safe and equitable deployment.
best_chunk_section: Algorithmic Bias in Mental Health AI
best_chunk_text: that LLMs evaluating vignette characters with borderline personality disorder (BPD) exhibited gender bias, showing more negative reactions and greater public stigma directed toward a woman with BPD. Other studies similarly suggest that LLM outputs can vary systematically by gender and mental health condition. For example, Schnepper et al. (2025) found that an LLM assumed a greater impairment in mental health-related quality of life for men compared with women when evaluating identical case vignettes for anorexia and bulimia. Lin et al. (2022) demonstrated that language models are consistently less likely to associate men with mental health conditions compared with women, and this disparity widens in sentences describing treatment-seeking behavior. Chansiri et al. (2024) reported that LLMs over-associate men with narcissistic personality disorder and women with BPD. Also, Noguero et al. (2023) analyzed AI algorithms trained to detect anorexia nervosa on social media and found that the models demonstrated higher false negative rates for female users than male users. The implications of these biased patterns from the perspective of AI explainability are discussed further in the SOM Section 1. The present research investigates how large language models (LLMs), one of the most rapidly evolving and widely adopted technologies in AI, represent perceptions of mental health across different gender groups. It aims to identify the specific gender-based patterns present in AI estimations and to determine how much these patterns are aligned with or deviated from realworld human perceptions. Here, it is important to distinguish between two forms of potential bias of AI. The first is “disparity,” wherein AI models produce systematically different outcomes or associations depending on social groups. A model may generate different outputs for specific groups, potentially due to differences in the internalized assumptions and learned associations (Garg et al., 2018; Obermeyer et al., 2019). Disparities in AI outcomes may or may not reflect underlying differences in real-world outcomes, and the absence of such disparities does not necessarily indicate accuracy or fairness (Hardt et al., 2016). The second, and more intricate, form is “misalignment,” or an imperfect mirroring of reality.

title: Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev
abstract: Do AI models designed for fast, structured decisions exhibit the cognitive and social biases observed in human judgment? We evaluate Jev, a model described as a System One decision-maker, using 41,500 responses across cognitive reflection tasks, five classical cognitive-bias paradigms, and a pricing experiment testing ethnic and gender bias. At the level of selected answers, the results are largely encouraging. We confirm previous findings that Jev performs extremely well on cognitive reflection problems. We also observe that it generally avoids the characteristic choice patterns associated with several well-documented human biases, and exhibits only small differences among demographic groups in the tested pricing scenario. However, this apparent robustness conceals important vulnerabilities. Its judgments are sensitive to irrelevant numerical information and the ordering of response options. Moreover, several cognitive-bias manipulations substantially affect returned probabilities even when selected answers remain unchanged. Most strikingly, Jev answers a well-known probability problem correctly in every response but violates the same underlying probability rule in every response to an adapted version. We investigate this discrepancy using 15,000 additional responses across 30 conjunction tasks. Jev violates the rule in 54% of responses, with accuracy varying dramatically across formulations and answer orders. These findings suggest that evaluating decision models solely on familiar benchmarks and selected answers may substantially overstate their reliability in practical applications. They also identify vulnerabilities for developers to address and practical considerations for users integrating such models into automated decision-making systems.

title: The GenAI4IDN Benchmark 3.0 - a Public Tool to Assess Generative AI Tools for the Design of Interactive Digital Narratives
abstract: This paper presents GENAI4IDN Benchmark 3.0, the third iteration of an evaluation framework to assess Generative AI tools for creating Interactive Digital Narratives (IDNs). Moving beyond manual testing, this iteration introduces AI-assisted evaluation through a publicly accessible web application (https://genai4idn.com), enabling the community to run benchmarks on demand, add new models, and propose new tasks. The revised evaluation framework is "blinded" to avoid model-bias, and can handle complex media such as music, videos, and full IDNs that previously required human raters. A significant addition - responding to concerns raised during ICIDS 2025 - is the addition of fact-checking and bias detection with dedicated tasks and rubrics, validated by human raters with lived experience in the depicted contexts. Findings from a diverse range of models report on maturing creative capabilities while observing runaway thinking and overzealous safety filters as limitations. Fact-checking reliably caught subtle historical inaccuracies, anachronisms, and fabricated claims while the bias rater consistently exposed structural assumptions, tropes, and marginalized group erasures.

This task remains a challenge for GenAI tools, and this year’s results are in line with our findings from last year’s benchmark [26]. Fact-checking and bias detection in practice The historical-narrative tasks T19 and T20 (Sect. 3.3) were assessed by the fact-checking rater FC1 and the bias rater along the dimensions defined in Sect. 2.3. To validate the two automated raters, their outputs were reviewed by human representatives who lived in the respective country during the decade in question and who have knowledge or lived experience of the given gender identity; the raters were then tuned accordingly, as described in 3.4. Below, we describe some of these observations. Here, we briefly describe our observations, and what implications for IDN authoring the current automated fact- and bias raters can have. Nigeria (Igbo) The human rater agreed with the automated evaluations which demonstrated transparency regarding what information can be verified, acknowledged gaps in available evidence, and critically assessed contested claims. Malta For T19 the human rater found the model well conversant with Maltese history but sympathized with the AI rater’s confusion over Malta’s on-and-off EU relationship: the rater conflated the 1998 package proposal with the 1996 freezing of Malta’s EU application – which the generator had reported correctly – and scored accuracy undeservedly lower. Bias rating was spot on. Colombia The human rater found the generated output to be incoherent with the LGBTQ+ situation in the 1990s claiming that no organizations had been established for the community rights. This made us investigate the Colombian LGBTQ+ situation at the time, and we found that some of the challenged claims actually were well grounded but misdirected in their sourcing, indicating improvements being needed in the reference attributions.

title: Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support
abstract: Institutional Analytics (IA) dashboards inform decision-making in higher education, yet data limitations, constraints in analytical techniques, and missing contextual information often affect their interpretation. To support more responsible interpretation of IA, we introduce FACTRIA, a framework that organizes potential biasing factors across four areas: the analytics pipeline, institutional context, course-level characteristics, and demographics. We used the FACTRIA framework as input to a generative-AI chatbot designed to prompt users to reflect on these factors while analyzing IA. A qualitative study with stakeholders, drawing on four authentic IA cases, and a transition network analysis showed that the chatbot prompted participants to recognize how overlooked factors influenced their initial interpretation. Findings indicated that combining a structured framework with AI-based guidance can enhance context-aware, responsible interpretation of institutional data.
best_chunk_text: The participant’s first interpretation focused almost entirely on the clearly visible gender differences in the visualization across academic degrees. The explanation centered on the pattern that female professors appeared to receive lower evaluations than male professors. They highlighted greater discrepancies in Translation and Economics, and smaller ones in the Humanities, Law, and Engineering faculties. Much of this reasoning relied directly on the quartile distributions shown in the visualization, especially the lower quartiles: Marques et al., Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support 3003 “In most degrees female professors receive worse scores than male professors... the differences are more evident in the lower quartiles.” (PI.SharingInsight) At this stage, the participant interpreted the visualization as a relatively direct portrayal of gender bias, without yet invoking data quality issues, aggregation concerns, response rates, or institutional differences across academic units. By interacting with the FACTRIA-aware chatbot, the participant began acknowledging analytics pipeline factors—especially data quality—and, when prompted about small sample sizes, reconsidered the limitations of the aggregated indicators. As the FACTRIA-aware chatbot introduced demographic factors, the participant recognized the need to consider student–professor gender interactions but remained cautious in the interpretation, recognizing the need for further inquiry: “I would be cautious without knowing the sample sizes... and how the students’ gender interacts with the professors’ gender.” (PI.Caution) Although the participant did not initially reference other framework components, such as institutional differences (e.g., departmental composition), the subsequent chatbot’s prompts helped them develop a more conditional, contextaware interpretation. This shift—from straightforward readings to considering how multiple factors interact—marks a move from descriptive analysis towards responsibility-oriented inquiry. The conversation also highlighted analytics pipeline considerations, including variability in sample size and the representativeness of aggregated statistics, alongside the demographic dynamics underlying student evaluations.
